# The Vanishing Dark

Two hours' drive from the nearest city, I pull the car onto a gravel shoulder and cut the engine. The sudden silence has a texture to it — the ticking of cooling metal, wind moving through dry grass, nothing else. Ahead of me is a darkness so total that at first I can't tell whether my eyes are open. There is a particular panic in that moment, brief and animal, the body insisting that sight has failed. Then shapes begin to assemble themselves out of nothing: the fence post, a bend in the road, the pale suggestion of a hillside. And above, once the sky finishes arriving — more stars than seem possible.

What follows is chemistry. The pupils widen as far as they can go within seconds, but that's the easy part. The real work happens in the retina, where a pigment called rhodopsin, bleached useless by every flashlight and phone screen of the day, slowly regenerates. Full dark adaptation takes twenty or thirty minutes. Stargazers guard this process jealously — they use red flashlights, dim dashboards, whisper to each other about luminous dials — because a single blast of white light from a passing car can reset the whole business, sending them back toward square one. Darkness is slow currency, earned minute by minute, and spendable in an instant.

Here is the strange truth of the present moment: most people will never do what I'm doing tonight, and many will never know what they're missing. The night has been quietly extinguished over the last century and a half, so gradually and so thoroughly that the loss became invisible even as it became universal. You cannot mourn, personally, a darkness you never stood inside. A third of humanity can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. In Europe and the United States, the figure climbs past ninety percent. The sky that every human being who ever lived before us took for granted — the ceiling of their imagination, their clock, their map, their news channel for everything divine — has become, for most of us, a rumor.

For the overwhelming majority of our species' history, night meant stars. Fire extended a small circle of warmth and vision, but beyond its radius lay the other country: vast, cold, glittering, alive with pattern. Our ancestors did not merely glance at that country. They inhabited it intellectually. The constellations were one of humanity's first databases — a way of storing stories, seasons, and directions in the only permanent structure available. You could burn a library, topple a monument, erase a border. Nobody could touch the sky.

And it functioned. Hesiod, writing practical farming advice nearly three thousand years ago, told Greek farmers to begin harvest when the Pleiades rose with the sun and to plow when they set — orbital mechanics rendered as almanac. On the other side of the planet, the rising of that same little cluster still marks Matariki, the Māori new year. Egyptian priests timed the annual Nile flood to the heliacal rising of Sirius and oriented temples to the rising points of stars. Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific holding courses by the positions of stars around the horizon at dawn and dusk, cross-checking against ocean swell patterns memorized like language. Enslaved people fleeing north through the American night reportedly steered partly by the Big Dipper — the "Drinking Gourd" of the songs — whose pointer stars lean toward Polaris, fixed in the north. The sky was infrastructure before it was poetry, and it kept working long after we forgot how much of our culture it was carrying.

Different peoples read different things in the same glitter. The Greeks assembled gods and beasts. Chinese astronomers charted a celestial bureaucracy, wall palaces and officialdom mirrored in heaven. Inca sky-readers found constellations in the dark patches themselves — clouds of interstellar dust shadowing the Milky Way's brightness, forming a celestial llama and other creatures made of shadow rather than light. Australian Aboriginal traditions likewise read the Emu in the darkness between stars. This is worth pausing on: some cultures looked into the deepest part of the night and saw not absence but figure, meaning drawn from what blocks the light. Those readings are only possible under a sky dark enough to show both terms — the light and its interruption.

Then Galileo pointed a tube at the hazy band. His *Sidereus Nuncius* reported in 1610 what had hung over every human head forever but had resisted close attention: the Milky Way was not vapor or river but, in his word, a mass of innumerable stars, each individually invisible alone, fused by distance into glow. Our own name for the galaxy preserves the older dreaminess — *galaxias kyklos*, the milky circle, spilt milk of a goddess across the heavens. What astronomy stripped of romance it repaid with staggering scale. Under a truly dark sky, you can see the Andromeda Galaxy without any instrument: a faint oval smear off the constellation's edge, the light of two and a half trillion suns compressed by distance to the apparent brightness of breath on glass. That light left home two and a half million years ago, before the genus Homo existed. Naked eyes, granted sufficient darkness, hold photons older than humanity. It is the longest look available to a creature without wings.

The dark began dying in 1807, when Pall Mall in London was illuminated by piped gas and crowds came to gawk at lamps burning without flame visibly consuming anything. Cities fell in love. Paris became the City of Light; the notion spread that brightness meant safety, prosperity, civilization itself. By the twentieth century the electric grid finished the job, and modernity has never looked back — or, more precisely, never stopped being unable to see behind it. Diarists during the wartime blackouts of the 1940s recorded their astonishment: Germans and Londoners alike, walking beneath temporarily dimmed skies, rediscovered stars their grandparents knew intimately. A century later, people in Los Angeles reportedly dialed emergency services after the 1994 earthquake knocked out power across the city, alarmed by a vast strange glow spreading overhead — the Milky Way, unfamiliar above their own neighborhood, mistaken for something ominous. Whether the exact calls happened quite as the story is told hardly matters; it survives because it rings true. We have produced generations who do not recognize their own galaxy.

The consequences run wider than nostalgia. Light pollution is an ecological force, and it kills. Sea turtle hatchlings, evolutionarily programmed to scramble toward the brighter horizon — which, on a natural beach, means the moonlit sea — crawl inland instead toward the neon wash of beachfront development, dying by the thousands in swimming pools and on roads. Moths, which appear to steer by celestial bodies held at constant angle, trace fatal logarithmic spirals into every unshielded bulb; the insects are harvested there in such quantities that lamps function as nutrient sinks, draining the night countryside to feed bats and birds gathered like beggars at a bottomless table. Fireflies, whose entire reproductive conversation is conducted in flashes tuned to darkness, lose each other in the glow like partners shouting at a rock concert. Corals synchronize their mass spawning by the moon; stray artificial light can knock them out of their window entirely. Migrating birds, drawn off course by urban skyglow, circle lit towers until they drop. Researchers studying New York's September 11 tribute lights — two columns of brilliance reaching four miles up — found hundreds of thousands of birds trapped in the beams, wheeling; the organizers now extinguish the lights for roughly twenty minutes whenever the trapped count climbs too high. Five minutes dark, and the birds scatter. The sky remembers how to be a highway.

Our own bodies didn't opt out either. A subset of cells in the human retina, discovered only decades ago, contains a light-sensitive protein called melanopsin, most sensitive to blue wavelengths — morning sky light, biologically speaking. Those cells feed the brain's master clock, suppressing melatonin and telling the body it is daytime. Artificial evenings saturated in blue-white LED are, from the perspective of these ancient cells, perpetual noon, and epidemiologists have linked chronic circadian disruption among night-shift workers to elevated risks of several diseases; international cancer agencies classify shift work involving circadian disruption as a probable carcinogen. None of this argues for abandoning electric light — ask anyone who has worked a night shift or walked home along a properly lit street what darkness-only policy would mean. It argues for intelligent light: warm in tone, aimed downward, timed when needed, dark when not. We light everything always, and the always is the problem.

Astronomers felt the erosion earliest and most bitterly. Observatories once built on convenient hills near towns watched those towns grow until their glow swallowed the survey's edge; Mount Wilson, where Edwin Hubble measured the expanding universe, now sits inside Los Angeles's dome of light, useful mainly for history. Professional astronomy retreated to mountaintops in deserts and ocean chains — the Atacama, Mauna Kea, the Canaries — the last reliably dark places, themselves increasingly contested by encroaching development. There is a bitter economics in it: a single poorly shielded parking lot luminaire costs a few hundred dollars and can degrade the view through a telescope whose construction cost millions. No one owns the light once it leaves the fixture. It trespasses endlessly, and until recently almost nowhere could you file a complaint against it.

The counterattack has been quieter but real. Flagstaff, Arizona, site of the observatory that discovered Pluto, became in 2001 the first International Dark Sky City, writing shielding requirements and strict brightness limits into municipal code. Natural Bridges National Monument in Utah was declared the world's first dark sky park in 2006; reserves multiplied thereafter across deserts, islands, and national parks — Cherry Springs in Pennsylvania draws amateur telescopes by the convoy; Aoraki Mackenzie in New Zealand markets its own darkness. Some of the Canary Islands legally restrict upward-directed light outright. Here is the remarkable part, the detail that should reframe everything: nearly every fix is cheap. Full-cutoff fixtures, dimmers, timers, motion sensors, warmer color temperatures — most measures pay for themselves in energy saved, because we currently blast photons everywhere continuously precisely because we aren't looking at what we're doing with them. Better lighting isn't worse lighting. The darkness advocates are asking for precision, not austerity. Light the door when someone approaches it; leave the rest of the county alone.

Back on the roadside, my eyes have finished their slow chemical work, and the sky has reached a depth the daytime mind struggles to credit. And it teaches one last small lesson in perception before I leave. The faintest things in the sky — the glow of the Milky Way's dusty rifts, distant smudges beyond counting — appear most plainly not when you look straight at them. The center of the retina is packed with cones, magnificent for daylight and color, nearly blind to faint glimmer. Sensitivity to dim light lives in the rod-rich periphery. So stargazers learn averted vision: glance slightly to the side of the object you wish to see, and watch it bloom. Look directly at the dimmest glow and it evaporates; look just past it, patiently, and it swims into view. There is an ethics buried in an eyeball. The subtlest things reveal themselves obliquely, to sideways attention, after a wait.

The winter Milky Way rises now like a column of smoke frozen mid-drift, the rift of dark dust down its spine exactly as the Inca sky-readers saw their shadow creatures in it. Orion leans above the hills, unfazed by being ignored for a century. The grass hisses. Somewhere north, a truck passes on a far highway, its sweep of headlights crossing the fields like a searchlight that finds nothing — and I feel my night-vision, that half hour of accumulated wealth, flicker and survive, dimmed a shade, then returning.

It would be easy to file all this under elegy, and some of it deserves to be filed there. But darkness is unlike nearly every other wilderness we've spent. The old forests, once clear-cut, take centuries to reassemble. Aquifers drain in decades and refill in geological time. The darkness is different. It renews completely, everywhere, instantly. Flip the switch — the shield goes on the fixture, the timer clicks over, the vanity floodlights stay off till eleven — and the oldest landscape we have returns that very night, undiminished, unmapped, exactly as it stood before electric light was a gleam in anyone's eye. Every extinction we cause is final except this one. Every habitat we poison stays poisoned, but the night forgives.

So the Milky Way is not gone. It's still there tonight over three hundred million backyards in this country alone, patient behind the skyglow, requiring nothing but a short drive and a longer willingness. Stand in it once and a permanent recalibration happens: a bodily knowledge that the world is larger than the lit part, that the day is not the whole of reality but the thin skin over it. The stars never went anywhere. Only our looking was switched off — and unlike them, unlike almost everything, that part we can fix ourselves, beginning with the next light bulb, and the next horizon, and the small act of looking slightly past the thing we think we want to see.

message.reasoning:
The user has given me complete freedom to write about whatever I want for 2500 words. This is an open-ended creative prompt. Let me think about what would make the most compelling piece of writing.

Options I'm considering:
1. A personal essay on some philosophical theme
2. A short story
3. A reflective meditation on something specific and textured
4. An essay about writing itself, AI, consciousness — though this might be too self-indulgent
5. Something about a specific place, experience, or idea

I think the best approach is to write something genuinely essayistic — a meditation that combines the personal, the observational, and the intellectual. The kind of thing a good essayist writes when given free rein. Let me brainstorm topics:

- Time and how we experience it
- Night and insomnia
- Maps and how they shape our sense of the world
- Libraries
- The sea
- Waiting rooms
- The history of silence
- Light pollution and the loss of darkness
- Walking as a practice of thought

Let me think about which of these can sustain 2500 words with genuine texture rather than padding.

I'm drawn to writing about darkness/the night sky/light pollution — it's rich territory: astronomy, history, ecology, human physiology, memory, wonder. Or maybe something more unexpected: the story of the "night" itself as an idea. Hmm.

Alternatively: waiting. We spend years of our lives waiting — in queues, in hospitals, at airports, for news. Waiting rooms are strange liminal spaces. That could be wonderful but might get repetitive.

Another idea: an essay on hands. Human hands — their evolution, their expression, everything we do with them, handshakes, craft, touch. That's surprisingly rich.

Or: the color blue. There's actually a great tradition here — William Gass wrote "On Being Blue." Blue is rare in nature (mostly structural color, not pigment), late to be named by human languages, the color of distance, melancholy, the sky's scattering of light... This could be beautiful.

Or: an essay about the ordinary miracle of tap water? Eh, less compelling.

Or something with narrative arc: a piece of fiction. A short story could showcase different muscles. But I think for freeform writing, a lyric-philosophical essay might land better — it can range widely and doesn't need plot mechanics.

Let me commit to darkness — night, light pollution, stars, the loss of the Milky Way from human experience. Actually, let me reconsider one more time between:

1. Darkness/night sky — strong sensory anchors, real science and history, emotional resonance (awe, loss), timely (80% of Americans can't see the Milky Way).
2. The color blue — also lovely but a bit done.
3. Waiting — good but harder to keep escalating.

Darkness it is. Let me plan the architecture so it builds rather than wanders:

Opening: Begin in medias res with a concrete scene — perhaps driving out to dark country, pulling over, killing the headlights, waiting for eyes to adjust. The ten-minute drama of dark adaptation. Sensory specifics: the dilation, rhodopsin, purkinje shift. Then pull back: most people never do this anymore.

Move into the history: For almost all of human existence, night was truly dark. Firelight was the only light. Then gaslight in the early 1800s (Pall Mall 1807, London), then electric light — cities that never sleep became literal. The night changed before our grandparents' grandparents' eyes.

The star registry of human culture: Every mythology was written against a dark sky. Farmers timed harvests by Pleiades (heliacal rising), Polynesian navigators read swells and stars across thousands of miles of ocean. Abraham Lincoln navigating by stars reading. Slaves escaping north followed the Drinking Gourd. The Underground Railroad. Ships dead reckoning under constellations. The sky was infrastructure — a clock, compass, calendar, almanac, cathedral.

Ecology: Light pollution kills. Moths spiraling to death around bulbs instead of pollinating night-blooming flowers. Baby sea turtles crawling toward hotel glow instead of moonlit surf. Birds colliding with lit towers; the Tribune Tower kill, 9/11 tribute lights study (the NYC memorial lights trap thousands of birds until lights are turned off periodically). Fireflies signaling in light noise like lovers trying to talk at a concert. Coral spawning synced to lunar cycle disrupted by artificial skylight. Human melatonin suppression; blue wavelengths hitting intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) containing melanopsin — the biology of why screens ruin sleep. Breast cancer / circadian disruption research, night-shift nurses studies.

Astronomy: professional observatories forced to remote mountaintops. Mount Wilson drowned in LA's glow. Flagstaff, Arizona — first International Dark Sky City because Lowell Observatory needed protection. Even there, LED retrogrades. Saturn through a telescope in a parking lot vs. a dark field — the difference awe makes.

Cultural/psychological: Loss of shared verticality — we look at screens not skies. When did you last see your shadow cast by the moon? Milky Way means "the river," many cultures saw it as a river of souls, road of birds, silver seam. Galileo turned his telescope on it and found it resolved into countless stars — "congeries of innumerable stars." Now a third of humanity including 80% of North Americans cannot see it. Big data point: 2016 Science Advances atlas — new Horizons-like analysis; world's population lives under light-polluted skies. Singapore is so bright people never fully dark-adapt ("Lightsprawl"?). I should be careful with precise stats — use ones I'm confident about: 2016 Falchi et al. atlas said 80% of North Americans cannot see the Milky Way, one-third of humanity. That's right.

Counter-movement: dark-sky places — Cherry Springs State Park, PA; Natural Bridges National Monument first dark sky park; Big Bend; Aoraki Mackenzie NZ; the Atacama; La Palma's sky law (light must be shielded, sodium low-pressure lamps). Light imposition vs. rights — the legal oddity that no one owns the beam once it leaves the fixture: "light trespass." Actually courts have dealt with nuisance claims over yard floodlights; amateurs in Tucson. Also interesting: fully shielded fixtures save money and see better — glare hides, darkness reveals. Crime data: more light doesn't clearly reduce crime; lighting can aid perpetrators (muggers need to see wallets too — that's somewhat cheeky; better: motion sensors beat all-night floods).

Personal scenes to weave: 
- Childhood memory: lying on garage roof or trampoline seeing Milky Way as "spilled sugar" — grandmother calling it.
- Blackout during the 1994 L.A. earthquake? People called 911 reporting a strange "giant silvery cloud" — the Milky Way. That's a famous anecdote, worth including: when power failed after the quake, some Angelenos called emergency services alarmed by the vast glowing sky above, not having seen the Milky Way before. It circulated widely; attributed often via the Griffith Observatory. I believe it is true enough and widely reported (e.g., associated with the 1994 Northridge earthquake). Include with light hedging ("a story astronomers tell," "reportedly").
- The war blackouts — city dwellers stunned by stars during WWII blackouts; Londoners reclaimed stars. Modern analog: La Palma lockdown? During COVID lockdowns skies dimmed over cities briefly.

Sensory/poetic middle: describe full dark adaptation — twenty minutes to a half hour; scotopic vision; peripheral vision catches faint things because rods are denser off-axis — "averted vision": looking slightly beside an object to see it — a nice metaphor: to see the faintest things you must look just past them. Use that as thematic pivot near end: our brightest instruments point away; the things we most want to perceive require indirect attention. Lovely.

Also the Andromeda galaxy — farthest thing visible to naked eye, 2.5 million light-years; light older than genus Homo. In a dark sky you see with unaided eye photons that left before humans existed. Under suburban glow, erasure of deep time.

Ending options: return to the roadside scene from opening — the narrator finally stands up stiff, sees the winter Milky Way arch overhead like steam, etc. Close with an exhortation not merely nostalgic: darkness isn't anti-progress; it's another form of wealth. Shielded lights, timers, amber wavelengths, curfews on vanity lighting — cheap fixes. And deeper point: we haven't lost the night; it's still there, a short drive away, patient. Darkness is renewable in a way nothing else is — turn off the switch and the oldest wilderness returns instantly, whole. End line possibilities: "Turn it off, and the oldest thing we have comes home." Something like: "Unlike nearly every other wilderness we've spent, this one refills the moment we stop spending it."

1. Roadside scene / dark adaptation (~350)
2. History of vanishing night (~300)
3. Sky as infrastructure & cultural memory (~400)
4. The blackout anecdotes / recent memory (~250)
5. Ecology of light (~350)

- Night and insomnia
- Maps and how they shape our sense of the world
- Libraries
- The sea
- Waiting rooms
- The history of silence

I'm drawn to writing about darkness/the night sky/light pollution — it's rich territory: astronomy, history, ecology, human physiology, memory, wonder. Or maybe something more unexpected: the story of the "night" itself as an idea. Hmm.

Alternatively: waiting. We spend years of our lives waiting — in queues, in hospitals, at airports, for news. Waiting rooms are strange liminal spaces. That could be wonderful but might get repetitive.

Another idea: an essay on hands. Human hands — their evolution, their expression, everything we do with them, handshakes, craft, touch. That's surprisingly rich.

Or: the color blue. There's actually a great tradition here — William Gass wrote "On Being Blue." Blue is rare in nature (mostly structural color, not pigment), late to be named by human languages, the color of distance, melancholy, the sky's scattering of light... This could be beautiful.

Or: an essay about the ordinary miracle of tap water? Eh, less compelling.

Or something with narrative arc: a piece of fiction. A short story could showcase different muscles. But I think for freeform writing, a lyric-philosophical essay might land better — it can range widely and doesn't need plot mechanics.

Let me commit to darkness — night, light pollution, stars, the loss of the Milky Way from human experience. Actually, let me reconsider one more time between:

1. Darkness/night sky — strong sensory anchors, real science and history, emotional resonance (awe, loss), timely (80% of Americans can't see the Milky Way).
2. The color blue — also lovely but a bit done.
3. Waiting — good but harder to keep escalating.

Sensory specifics: the dilation, rhodopsin, purkinje shift. Then pull back: most people never do this anymore.

Move into the history: For almost all of human existence, night was truly dark. Firelight was the only light. Then gaslight in the early 1800s (Pall Mall 1807, London), then electric light — cities that never sleep became literal. The night changed before our grandparents' grandparents' eyes.

The star registry of human culture: Every mythology was written against a dark sky. Farmers timed harvests by Pleiades (heliacal rising), Polynesian navigators read swells and stars across thousands of miles of ocean. Abraham Lincoln navigating by stars reading. Slaves escaping north followed the Drinking Gourd. The Underground Railroad. Ships dead reckoning under constellations. The sky was infrastructure — a clock, compass, calendar, almanac, cathedral.

Ecology: Light pollution kills. Moths spiraling to death around bulbs instead of pollinating night-blooming flowers. Baby sea turtles crawling toward hotel glow instead of moonlit surf. Birds colliding with lit towers; the Tribune Tower kill, 9/11 tribute lights study (the NYC memorial lights trap thousands of birds until lights are turned off periodically). Fireflies signaling in light noise like lovers trying to talk at a concert. Coral spawning synced to lunar cycle disrupted by artificial skylight. Human melatonin suppression; blue wavelengths hitting intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) containing melanopsin — the biology of why screens ruin sleep. Breast cancer / circadian disruption research, night-shift nurses studies.

Astronomy: professional observatories forced to remote mountaintops. Mount Wilson drowned in LA's glow. Flagstaff, Arizona — first International Dark Sky City because Lowell Observatory needed protection. Even there, LED retrogrades. Saturn through a telescope in a parking lot vs. a dark field — the difference awe makes.

Cultural/psychological: Loss of shared verticality — we look at screens not skies. When did you last see your shadow cast by the moon? Milky Way means "the river," many cultures saw it as a river of souls, road of birds, silver seam. Galileo turned his telescope on it and found it resolved into countless stars — "congeries of innumerable stars." Now a third of humanity including 80% of North Americans cannot see it. Big data point: 2016 Science Advances atlas — new Horizons-like analysis; world's population lives under light-polluted skies. Singapore is so bright people never fully dark-adapt ("Lightsprawl"?). I should be careful with precise stats — use ones I'm confident about: 2016 Falchi et al. atlas said 80% of North Americans cannot see the Milky Way, one-third of humanity. That's right.

Counter-movement: dark-sky places — Cherry Springs State Park, PA; Natural Bridges National Monument first dark sky park; Big Bend; Aoraki Mackenzie NZ; the Atacama; La Palma's sky law (light must be shielded, sodium low-pressure lamps). Light imposition vs. rights — the legal oddity that no one owns the beam once it leaves the fixture: "light trespass." Actually courts have dealt with nuisance claims over yard floodlights; amateurs in Tucson. Also interesting: fully shielded fixtures save money and see better — glare hides, darkness reveals. Crime data: more light doesn't clearly reduce crime; lighting can aid perpetrators (muggers need to see wallets too — that's somewhat cheeky; better: motion sensors beat all-night floods).

- Childhood memory: lying on garage roof or trampoline seeing Milky Way as "spilled sugar" — grandmother calling it.
- Blackout during the 1994 L.A. earthquake? People called 911 reporting a strange "giant silvery cloud" — the Milky Way. That's a famous anecdote, worth including: when power failed after the quake, some Angelenos called emergency services alarmed by the vast glowing sky above, not having seen the Milky Way before. It circulated widely; attributed often via the Griffith Observatory. I believe it is true enough and widely reported (e.g., associated with the 1994 Northridge earthquake). Include with light hedging ("a story astronomers tell," "reportedly").
- The war blackouts — city dwellers stunned by stars during WWII blackouts; Londoners reclaimed stars. Modern analog: La Palma lockdown? During COVID lockdowns skies dimmed over cities briefly.

Sensory/poetic middle: describe full dark adaptation — twenty minutes to a half hour; scotopic vision; peripheral vision catches faint things because rods are denser off-axis — "averted vision": looking slightly beside an object to see it — a nice metaphor: to see the faintest things you must look just past them. Use that as thematic pivot near end: our brightest instruments point away; the things we most want to perceive require indirect attention. Lovely.

Also the Andromeda galaxy — farthest thing visible to naked eye, 2.5 million light-years; light older than genus Homo. In a dark sky you see with unaided eye photons that left before humans existed. Under suburban glow, erasure of deep time.

Ending options: return to the roadside scene from opening — the narrator finally stands up stiff, sees the winter Milky Way arch overhead like steam, etc. Close with an exhortation not merely nostalgic: darkness isn't anti-progress; it's another form of wealth. Shielded lights, timers, amber wavelengths, curfews on vanity lighting — cheap fixes. And deeper point: we haven't lost the night; it's still there, a short drive away, patient. Darkness is renewable in a way nothing else is — turn off the switch and the oldest wilderness returns instantly, whole. End line possibilities: "Turn it off, and the oldest thing we have comes home." Something like: "Unlike nearly every other wilderness we've spent, this one refills the moment we stop spending it."
